sections.heading: C — Winter Danger Spots, Dawn and Night Driving, Freeway Driving and Emergency Procedures
sections.markdown:
## C — Winter Danger Spots, Dawn and Night Driving, Freeway Driving and Emergency Procedures

FACT_ID: sec15-F01 | anchor: A01
In winter conditions a bridge deck or the road beneath it can ice over while the surrounding road stays clear, shaded stretches hold snow and ice longer, and a shiny patch on the road may be ice [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec15-F02 | anchor: A01
On packed snow or ice use the brakes very cautiously and intermittently, because locked wheels mean loss of control, and steer into a clear area if a collision seems imminent [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec15-F03 | anchor: A01
When driving toward the rising or setting sun use the sun visors and sunglasses and keep the windshield and windows absolutely clean to cut glare, and in the dim period just before sunrise and after sunset, worse under a cloudy sky, turn on the low-beam head lamps so others can see you and watch for unlighted objects and pedestrians [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec15-F04 | anchor: A01
No one sees as well at night as in daylight, and alternating light and darkness keeps a driver from reaching full night seeing ability, so protect your eyes from bright light for several hours before a night drive and clean the windshield and windows inside and out [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec15-F05 | anchor: A01
At night make sure every lamp works, reduce speed so you can stop within the distance you can see ahead, and never use high beams when approaching or following other vehicles [A01].
Why it matters: stopping within the lit distance is the night speed rule.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec15-F06 | anchor: A01
If an approaching vehicle's lights are too bright, flash your high beams once and look toward the right edge of the road, using lane markings or reflectors as a guide, and remember that red lane reflectors mean you are going the wrong way in the lane [A01].
Why it matters: red reflectors facing you are the wrong-way warning.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec15-F07 | anchor: A01
Freeways are safe high-speed roads because they have no steep hills or sharp curves to limit sight distance, no stop signs, signals or railroad crossings, and entrances and exits only at planned locations, so their driving has its own procedures [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec15-F08 | anchor: A02
Plan a freeway trip with a map, knowing exactly where you will enter and leave, and make sure the vehicle has enough gasoline, oil, water and good tires, because service stations are off the freeway and a breakdown on the freeway can create an extremely dangerous situation [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec15-F09 | anchor: A02
To enter a freeway follow the signs to the correct entrance, and if the entrance lane is congested slow down or stop near its beginning rather than creeping to the end of the entrance lane and stopping, because merging from a stop at the end of the ramp is very difficult and dangerous [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec15-F10 | anchor: A02
When the entrance lane is clear, signal your merge, accelerate to match freeway traffic, and if the near lane is clear move into it and hold your speed, but if vehicles are coming, slow slightly and move in behind them [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec15-F11 | anchor: A03
On the freeway watch all signs, through traffic uses the left or center lanes at or near the posted limit, the right lane is for vehicles that cannot keep up and should stay open as much as possible for entering and leaving traffic, and a right-lane driver leaves space for entering vehicles [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec15-F12 | anchor: A03
Avoid lane changes on the freeway, signal well ahead of any you make, use the mirrors and look back first, never stop unless absolutely unavoidable, never slow unnecessarily, and never follow too closely, because freeway rear-end collisions are common and usually involve several vehicles [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec15-F13 | anchor: A03
Never cross a freeway center divider, turn around or back up on a freeway; if you must go the other way, drive to the next exit, leave and re-enter in the opposite direction [A03].
Why it matters: the three nevers, cross, turn around, back up, are the core freeway rule.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec15-F14 | anchor: A03
For an emergency stop try to reach the next exit, otherwise drive entirely off the roadway as far from traffic as possible, never stand or walk on the freeway, and do not stop to help other drivers in trouble but report them to the proper authorities [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec15-F15 | anchor: A04
To leave the freeway watch the exit signs, signal, move into the exit lane, keep your speed until you are completely on the exit ramp and then slow smoothly, and if you miss your exit never stop or back up but continue to the next exit [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec15-F16 | anchor: A04
Every driving emergency involves brakes, steering and power, so stay calm, never slam the brakes into a wheel slide because a sliding vehicle cannot be controlled, and steer toward the least dangerous place available [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec15-F17 | anchor: A04
In an emergency apply maximum braking without sliding the wheels, releasing and reapplying the brakes if any wheel slides, which antilock brakes do automatically, wear your belt so you stay in position to control the vehicle, and keep trying to control it even after striking something [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec15-F18 | anchor: A04
A tire blowout is the sudden release of air that collapses a tire and can cause loss of control, it most often results from poor tire care, so check pressure and condition every month [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec15-F19 | anchor: A05
In a blowout do not apply the brakes, which can make the vehicle uncontrollable; grip the wheel firmly and steer to stay in your lane against a pull that may go either way, slow gradually without the brakes until very slow, then brake lightly and pull off into a safe area, since a blown tire can be driven slowly for some distance without damaging the rim [A05].
Why it matters: no brakes at first is the counter-intuitive step tested most.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec15-F20 | anchor: A05
Losing a wheel is uncommon but is handled like a blowout, partial or total brake failure is likely when it happens, and once stopped the vehicle cannot be moved and must be towed [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec15-F21 | anchor: A05
Total brake failure is very unlikely on a modern car because the service brake system almost always keeps partial braking, and a partial failure shows as reduced braking and a warning light on the panel [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0081]

sections.heading: C — Winter Danger Spots, Dawn and Night Driving, Freeway Driving and Emergency Procedures (continued)
sections.markdown:
## C — Winter Danger Spots, Dawn and Night Driving, Freeway Driving and Emergency Procedures (continued)

FACT_ID: sec15-F22 | anchor: A05
If the brakes fail completely, pump the pedal quickly, shift to a lower gear, look for an escape route such as a side road or flat open area while warning others with lights and horn, and apply the parking brake gradually, never rapidly or with great force, until you stop [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec15-F23 | anchor: A05
Complete steering failure almost never happens on a well-maintained vehicle, but a partial loss can occur with power steering, in which case you must apply greater effort to the wheel and never give up on steering [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec15-F24 | anchor: A06
If the steering fails completely, slowly reduce speed and use the brakes as needed to avoid striking anything, stopping as smoothly as possible [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec15-F25 | anchor: A06
If your wheels drop off the pavement edge, do not jerk the wheel to force the vehicle back, because gravel, dirt or the pavement lip resists a smooth return; keep driving with the wheels off the pavement, slow down, brake gently, and at a safe speed steer back onto the pavement ready to correct immediately to stay in your lane [A06].
Why it matters: the error the manual warns against is yanking the wheel back at speed.
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec15-F26 | anchor: A06
If a vehicle passing you cannot complete the pass because of oncoming traffic, steer as far right as is safe, even onto the shoulder, and then either slow so the passer can pull in ahead or, if the passer seems to be dropping back, accelerate so it can return behind you, after making sure of the other driver's intention [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec15-F27 | anchor: A06
If an oncoming vehicle is in your lane, flash your lights and sound the horn, quickly slow and steer right out of the lane into any clear area, even off the road while avoiding solid objects and pedestrians, and never swerve into the oncoming lane [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec15-F28 | anchor: A06
A stuck accelerator keeps the vehicle at speed or accelerating after your foot is lifted, and it often develops right after the pedal has been pushed fully down [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec15-F29 | anchor: A07
For a stuck accelerator slap the pedal hard, quickly pressing and releasing it, turn the ignition only far enough to stop the engine without engaging the steering lock, expecting heavier steering and braking effort, apply the brakes and pull off into a safe area [A07].
Why it matters: turning the key too far locks the steering, which is the trap in this procedure.
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec15-F30 | anchor: A07
Power steering failure usually comes with engine failure or a lost drive belt, requires extra effort to keep steering control, and calls for reducing speed and driving to a safe area to stop [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec15-F31 | anchor: A07
Most skids come from sudden changes of direction or speed, with excessive speed for road and traffic conditions the most common cause, so take extra care on wet, slippery or gravel-covered surfaces and correct a skid immediately and smoothly before control is lost [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec15-F32 | anchor: A07
When a skid or control problem starts, stop or reduce whatever you were doing when it began, avoid the brakes and release them if braking started the skid, and ease off the accelerator, which may end the skid by itself [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec15-F33 | anchor: A07
To steer out of a skid, turn the wheel firmly but not sharply in the direction the rear of the vehicle is sliding, right for a skid to the right and left for a skid to the left, straighten as the skid stops, and if overcorrection starts a skid the other way, steer gently into that skid and repeat until you have control [A07].
Why it matters: steer the way the rear is going, and expect to repeat gently against an overcorrection.
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec15-F34 | anchor: A08
Vehicle fires usually start with an engine that has overheated, a short in the electrical system, or a leak of fuel or oil, and any burning odor should be investigated at once [A08].
Source: [A08 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec15-F35 | anchor: A08
If fire occurs or is suspected, drive to a safe area clear of traffic and stop, turn off the ignition and every electrical switch, and get all occupants out, away from the vehicle and off the roadway because poisonous fumes can fill the vehicle quickly [A08].
Source: [A08 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec15-F36 | anchor: A08
Smother a small fire with an extinguisher, dirt, sand or a blanket, never use water on a gasoline, oil or electrical fire, and do not try to fight a large gasoline or oil fire but seek assistance [A08].
Source: [A08 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec15-F37 | anchor: A08
Most breakdowns are not dangerous in themselves but can leave the vehicle stalled in a hazardous position, so move it to a safe spot if possible, keep occupants away from traffic by moving them to a reachable safe location, and otherwise keep them inside the vehicle [A08].
Source: [A08 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec15-F38 | anchor: A08
After a breakdown use hazard lights, flares, warning reflectors and a flashlight, which should always be carried, stay locked in the vehicle until sure of a helper's intentions and ask that the police be notified if in doubt, and signal for help by raising the hood and tying a white cloth to the antenna or door handle [A08].
Source: [A08 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec15-F39 | anchor: A08
If you must leave a broken-down vehicle, lock it and return as soon as practicable, walk facing traffic and well clear of the roadway if you must walk along a highway, and never walk on a freeway but stay with the vehicle until help arrives [A08].
Source: [A08 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0084]

Misconceptions: in a blowout you do not brake first, you steer and let the speed fall; off the pavement edge you do not jerk the wheel back; in a skid you steer the way the rear is sliding and stay off the brakes; with a stuck accelerator the key is turned only far enough to stop the engine, never to the lock position; water is never used on a gasoline, oil or electrical fire; a missed freeway exit means continuing to the next one, never stopping or backing; if an oncoming car is in your lane you go right, never into the oncoming lane.

Mnemonics: Blowout: grip, steer, coast, then brake; skid: off the brakes, off the gas, steer where the rear goes; freeway: never cross, never turn around, never back up; fire: stop, switch off, get out, smother small ones, never water.

Glossary: blowout (the sudden collapse of a tire from loss of air); escape route (a side road or open area used to stop a car whose brakes have failed); steering lock (the ignition position that locks the wheel, to be avoided when stopping a runaway engine); skid (loss of tire grip from a sudden change of speed or direction); overcorrecting (steering too far in a skid and starting one the other way); center divider (the barrier between freeway directions that must never be crossed).

Dynamic facts: none; emergency procedures and freeway rules are stable teaching content of this printing.

items.why: the chapter teaches each emergency as an ordered procedure with a forbidden first move, such as not braking in a blowout or not jerking the wheel off the pavement edge, so a learner must choose the right response to a described situation, not only recall a list

corpus_stability.reason: The Hawaii Driver's Manual is a periodically reprinted reference (imprint HMG 5/2023, copyright line through 2023); the icy danger spots, dawn and dusk glare, night driving precautions, freeway planning, entering, driving, emergency stops and exiting, and the emergency procedures for blowouts, lost wheels, brake and steering failure, wheels off the pavement, passing conflicts, oncoming vehicles, a stuck accelerator, skids, fire and breakdowns rules on pages 77–84 are statutory and procedural content that changes less than once a year, so no BlockedProbe.
